job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
**Drafting review of S. 2817 (text as amended October 6, 2026)**

I'm working only from the text you pasted. I can't check it against the official bill text on Congress.gov, so confirm the wording against the committee print before anything runs in print.

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "by a single vessel":** A mining operation can use several vessels that each recover under 10,000 metric tons per year, so the threshold can be avoided by splitting the operation across a fleet.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "10,000 metric tons per year":** The bill doesn't say how tonnage is measured (wet or dry weight, nodules or processed ore, per vessel or per operator, calendar or rolling year), which makes the threshold easy to contest.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "at depths greater than 200 meters":** The bill doesn't say where depth is measured (at the recovery site, the vessel, or the seabed), and the threshold excludes shallower recovery.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources" and "seabed":** "Mineral resources" and "seabed" are undefined, so it's unclear whether the bill covers cobalt crusts, seafloor massive sulfides, or sub-seabed extraction.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(B), "the Secretary determines" and "comparable":** The bill doesn't say which Secretary decides, and "comparable" has no standard, procedure, notice requirement, or review mechanism. This invites APA challenges and vagueness arguments, which matter most because Sec. 5(b) attaches criminal penalties to the prohibition.

6. **Sec. 2(2), "U.S. person":** The definition covers state-incorporated corporations and citizens only, which leaves out LLCs, partnerships, trusts, foreign subsidiaries of U.S. firms, and permanent residents, and it doesn't cross-reference a definition of "person."

7. **Sec. 2(3), "equipped for the recovery":** "Equipped" is undefined, so a vessel can conduct mining without being "equipped" in the sense the bill requires, and the 5,000-gross-ton cutoff is not tied to any mining capacity.

8. **Sec. 3(a), "engage in":** The bill doesn't define "engage in," so it's unclear whether it covers financing, equipment supply, processing, or purchase and import of recovered minerals.

9. **Sec. 3(a), extraterritorial reach:** The prohibition covers persons "in the United States" and U.S. persons "anywhere," but foreign-flagged vessels or foreign-incorporated affiliates operating outside U.S. jurisdiction fall outside it.

10. **Sec. 3(b), "exploration license":** The bill doesn't identify which licenses qualify, and the statute has no federal "exploration license" category for deep seabed mining. Read literally, the clause could let an exploration license cover commercial recovery.

11. **Sec. 3(b), grandfather clause scope:** The exemption has no time limit, volume cap, or expiration, and it doesn't address renewals, transfers, or amendments after enactment.

12. **Sec. 3(b) and Sec. 8, timing:** The grandfather clause keys to the date of enactment, but the prohibition takes effect 180 days later. That gap creates an incentive to obtain licenses during the 180-day window.

13. **Sec. 3(c), "for the purpose of environmental assessment":** "Purpose" is subjective, and the bill sets no limit on material recovered, no permit, and no reporting, so commercial-scale recovery could be labeled "assessment."

14. **Sec. 4(a), "operator":** "Operator" is undefined and may not match the owner or the party that controls the vessel. The bill also sets no registration deadline and no content requirements for the registry.

15. **Sec. 4(b), "recovery activities":** The quarterly report doesn't specify what must be reported (tonnage, location, depth, dates), so the 10,000-ton threshold can't be verified. The report is also self-certified, with no verification and no false-statement provision.

16. **Sec. 4 versus Sec. 5, missing penalties:** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so failing to register or to file reports carries no penalty. Enforcement of Sec. 4 depends on other law that the bill doesn't cite.

17. **Sec. 4 and Sec. 2(3), coverage gap:** Registration and reporting apply only to covered vessels (over 5,000 gross tons), but the prohibition in Sec. 3 applies to all commercial mining, so smaller vessels can mine without registering or reporting.

18. **Sec. 5(a) versus Sec. 8, effective date conflict:** Sec. 5(a) covers violations "on or after the date of enactment," but Sec. 8 delays the Act's effect by 180 days, so it's unclear whether conduct during that window is penalized.

19. **Sec. 5(a), "each day on which the violation occurs":** The bill doesn't define how days are counted for continuing violations, per-vessel violations, or multi-vessel operations, and it sets no inflation adjustment.

20. **Sec. 5, enforcement mechanics:** The bill doesn't designate an enforcing agency, specify administrative versus judicial procedures, provide injunctive authority, or authorize vessel seizure or forfeiture, and it doesn't address whether penalties can reach a vessel itself.

21. **Sec. 5(b), "willfully":** "Willfully" is undefined, and the bill doesn't address corporate officer liability or extraterritorial criminal jurisdiction over foreign persons acting abroad.

22. **Sec. 6, "shall seek to negotiate":** The duty is to try, not to conclude an agreement, and the bill sets no reporting to Congress and no consequence for failure. "Equivalent to those in section 3" is also vague, and the bill doesn't say how the agreement interacts with the International Seabed Authority or UNCLOS.

23. **Sec. 7(a), "serious harm":** The "without serious harm" standard is undefined, and the bill doesn't set a deadline for the NASEM report, specify what it must contain, or specify how the joint resolution is handled (including presentment to the President).

24. **Sec. 7(b), sunset versus Sec. 7(a):** The sunset ends the entire Act after 10 years, which makes the open-ended prohibition in Sec. 7(a) moot at that point. Because the prohibition takes effect 180 days after enactment, the operative period is closer to 9.5 years.

25. **Sec. 7(b), no savings clause:** Nothing addresses whether penalties accrued, enforcement actions pending, or violations committed before the sunset survive it.

26. **Missing general provisions:** The bill has no severability clause, no rulemaking authority, no judicial review provision, no preemption or savings clause for state law, and no reference to the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act of 1980. That 1980 law already licenses U.S. citizens for seabed mining, so the bill needs to say whether it repeals, amends, or overrides those licenses.

27. **Missing jurisdictional clarification:** The bill doesn't say whether it applies to mining on the U.S. continental shelf or Outer Continental Shelf, which is governed by OCSLA and BOEM, or whether it reaches state waters. "Deep seabed" in U.S. jurisdiction could mean several different regimes.

**Priorities for the markup:** The most consequential items for loophole and enforceability questions are the single-vessel threshold (1), the undefined "Secretary" and "comparable" standard (5), the exploration-license grandfather clause (10–12), the penalty gap for Sec. 4 (16), the effective-date conflict (18), and the sunset interaction with Sec. 7(a) (24). Item 26's DSHMRA interaction may also be a question staff can put to committee counsel or the sponsor's office before Thursday.
